content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define electroplating and explain its purpose
Describe how electroplating is carried out
Identify the cathode, anode, and electrolyte used
Give examples of uses of electroplating
uses electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal. This process is widely used in industry to improve appearance, prevent corrosion, or add special properties to objects.
The process of using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal.
Make objects look more attractive (e.g., silver or gold plating)
Use cheap metal underneath, expensive metal on surface
The object to be plated is always the cathode (negative electrode).
[DIAGRAM: Electroplating setup showing: cathode (object to be plated), anode (plating metal), electrolyte (solution of plating metal salt), power supply]
Solution containing ions of the plating metal
The object to be plated is connected as the cathode
A piece of the plating metal is connected as the anode
Both electrodes are placed in a solution containing ions of the plating metal
At cathode: Metal ions gain electrons and deposit on the object
At anode: Metal atoms lose electrons and go into solution
Silver dissolves to replace the ions used
Silver is transferred from the anode to the spoon. The anode gets smaller, the spoon gains a silver coating.
Higher current = faster plating (but may be uneven)
Clean the object thoroughly (remove grease, dirt, oxide layer)
May need to acid-wash or sand the surface
Sometimes plate with copper first (better adhesion)
Use low current for even coating
May need to rotate or move the object
The amount of metal deposited depends on:
The charge on the metal ion
More current × more time = more metal deposited
Describe how to electroplate a steel key with copper.
Connect the key to the negative terminal of the power supply (cathode)
Connect a piece of pure copper to the positive terminal (anode)
Place both in copper sulfate solution (electrolyte)
At the cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper deposits on key)
At the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (copper dissolves)
Remove key when desired thickness achieved
A piece of jewellery is to be gold plated. State what should be used as:
a) Cathode: The piece of jewellery (the object to be plated)
c) Electrolyte: Gold chloride solution (or another gold salt solution)
Explain why the anode gets smaller during electroplating.
The anode is made of the plating metal
At the anode, metal atoms lose electrons
Metal atoms become metal ions and dissolve into the solution
The anode gradually decreases in size as metal is transferred
This maintains the concentration of metal ions in the electrolyte
Why must the object be thoroughly cleaned before electroplating?
Grease, dirt, or oxide layers prevent good adhesion
The plating metal won't bond properly to a dirty surface
The coating may be uneven or flake off
A clean surface ensures an even, strongly bonded coating
Putting the object to be plated at the anode
The object must be the CATHODE (negative) - that's where metal deposits
Using any solution as the electrolyte
The electrolyte must contain ions of the PLATING metal
Thinking electroplating creates a thick layer
Electroplating produces a THIN coating (μm to mm)
